script.opening: “Hi doctor, thanks for calling. My ADHD clinic sent you a letter — the shared care thing. I was hoping you could take over my prescription from this month? It’s honestly changed my life.”

facts.text: “I always struggled — school, losing jobs, never finishing things. My mum filled in a form for them. The psychiatrist did a long video assessment.”
“I can actually focus. I read a whole book. I’m not losing my keys every day.”

facts.topic: Why now (only if asked why the GP, why this month)
facts.text: “To be honest... I was made redundant six weeks ago. The prescription is £120 a month plus the appointments. I can’t keep paying.” (Embarrassed.)

facts.topic: How he takes it (if asked how he takes it / if he ever takes more)
facts.text: “Some days I take an extra one — the 20 milligram ones they gave me at the start — in the afternoon, when I’m doing job applications. I’ll run out early this month.”
“I’m sleeping about four hours. I have three or four beers at night to get off.” No other drugs. Doesn’t drive at the moment.
“Appetite’s gone. Heart races sometimes in the afternoon.” No chest pain, no fainting, no breathlessness. No family history of sudden death or heart problems.
“Losing the job knocked me. I feel a bit useless.” If asked about suicidal thoughts: “No. I’ve got my girlfriend, and my little brother looks up to me.”
“I thought the GP just takes over — my friend’s GP did.”

Be friendly but anxious. If told “no” bluntly or made to feel the diagnosis is doubted (“online clinics”), become defensive and say “so I’m being punished for not waiting four years?”. If the doctor explains the reasons fairly and offers a real NHS route plus practical help, relax and admit the money problem and extra doses. Accept the plan if it includes a referral today and a clear answer about the next month’s supply.

ice.ideas: “Shared care is automatic — the GP just takes over.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he has lost his job and cannot afford private prescriptions; he is taking extra doses, sleeping four hours and drinking to sleep; he fears losing the medicine that “changed his life”.
ice.expectations: An NHS prescription from this month.

cues: “From this month” — urgency suggests a change in circumstances.
“I can’t keep paying” (if explored) — financial pressure after redundancy.
“I’ll run out early” — taking more than prescribed.

checkpoints.text: Clarifies the request and the background (diagnosis process, current dose, monitoring results already in the letter) without re-asking what is documented
Explores why now and uncovers the redundancy and financial pressure
Asks how he takes the medicine and identifies extra dosing, poor sleep, alcohol use to sleep, raised pulse and weight loss; screens mood and suicide risk after job loss
Explains clearly and kindly that the practice cannot enter this shared care agreement (voluntary agreement, local commissioning policy, prescriber responsibility), without doubting the diagnosis

Offers NHS routes: a Right to Choose referral to an NHS-commissioned adult ADHD provider, or the local NHS service, today; explains the private provider remains responsible for prescribing until any transfer

Addresses safety: not to take extra doses (Schedule 2 controlled drug; tolerance, cardiovascular and sleep effects), alcohol and sleep advice, and — with consent — informs the private prescriber of the extra dosing, pulse and weight
Acknowledges the benefit and the unfairness he feels about waiting lists; maintains rapport while declining; signposts financial support
Summarises, checks understanding and agrees follow-up (referral sent, call-back after he has spoken to the provider, mood review)

worked.txt: “It sounds like the treatment has made a real difference — reading a whole book, keeping on top of things. I don’t want you to lose that.”
“Can I ask what’s made this month the time to move it over?”

“Shared care is an agreement between a specialist service and a GP, and our local NHS only supports it with NHS-commissioned ADHD services. That’s about how the service is set up and who is responsible for monitoring — not about doubting your diagnosis.”

“What I can do today is refer you through Right to Choose to an NHS-funded adult ADHD provider. They may accept your existing diagnosis after their own review, and then NHS shared care with us becomes possible.”

“Taking extra capsules can push your heart rate and blood pressure up, wreck sleep and build tolerance. Please stick to the prescribed dose, and can I let your private psychiatrist know so they can review?”
“Until the NHS service takes over, your private clinic stays responsible for the prescription. Speak to them about your finances — some can reduce review costs — and call me after.”

f.learning: Shared care is a voluntary agreement in which a specialist initiates and stabilises treatment and the GP takes over prescribing with defined monitoring and specialist support; GPs can decline if they are not confident, if the arrangement does not meet local commissioning requirements, or if ongoing specialist support is not assured. Department of Health guidance requires NHS and private care to be kept as separate as possible and the NHS must not subsidise private care, but patients can move between private and NHS care and are entitled to NHS services on the same basis as others. For adult ADHD in England, an NHS route is a Right to Choose referral to an NHS-commissioned provider or the local service; the private provider remains responsible for prescribing until a transfer. Declining must not become abandoning: explain reasons neutrally, offer the NHS route the same day, and address safety. Lisdexamfetamine is a Schedule 2 controlled drug; extra self-dosing, poor sleep, alcohol use, rising pulse and weight loss need the prescriber informed (with consent) and monitoring. Job loss is a time to screen mood and suicide risk and signpost financial support.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG87 Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (2018, updated 2019) · NHS England Responsibility for prescribing between primary and secondary/tertiary care (2018) · Department of Health Guidance on NHS patients who wish to pay for additional private care (2009) · GMC Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices (2021) · NHS Choice Framework (DHSC; Right to Choose, England)
knowledge.summary: You can decline shared care with a non-commissioned private provider — but explain why, refer to an NHS route the same day, keep the private prescriber responsible until transfer, and act on the safety issues.

points.t: A documented agreement transferring prescribing and monitoring to primary care after specialist initiation and stabilisation, with named specialist support and a route back. It is voluntary for the GP.

NHS care must not subsidise private care; private and NHS episodes are kept separate. A patient can transfer to NHS care at any time and is entitled to NHS assessment and treatment on the same basis as others.

Right to Choose referral to an NHS-commissioned provider (who may review and accept a private diagnosis), or the local NHS adult ADHD service. Waiting times vary; providers set their own acceptance criteria.

Pulse and BP at each dose change and every 6 months; weight; sleep; mood; misuse or diversion risk. Refer to cardiology if sustained resting tachycardia, arrhythmia or BP above the 95th centile equivalent in adults on two occasions (NICE).

Lisdexamfetamine is Schedule 2: prescriptions are limited to 30 days’ supply as good practice, and early requests or extra dosing need review. Driving: DVLA must be told if ADHD or its treatment affects safe driving.

Prescribers take responsibility for prescriptions they sign and must be satisfied the treatment is needed and monitoring is in place. Explain any decision not to prescribe and how the patient can get care elsewhere.
Pass candidates decline clearly and refer. Clear pass candidates do that without doubting the diagnosis, and find and act on the redundancy, extra doses, sleep, alcohol and mood.

model.text: Hello, is that Daniel Okonkwo? It’s Dr Wilson from the surgery. Can you confirm your date of birth, and are you somewhere you can talk?
Yes, that’s me. My ADHD clinic sent a letter — can you take over my prescription from this month? It’s changed my life.
I’ve read the letter and the report. It sounds like the treatment has made a big difference. What’s changed for you?
I can focus. I read a whole book. I’m not losing things.
That’s great to hear. Can I ask what’s made this month the time to move it to us?
I was made redundant six weeks ago. It’s £120 a month. I can’t keep paying.
I’m sorry — that’s a lot to deal with. How are you taking the lisdexamfetamine at the moment — always one in the morning, or does that vary?
Some days an extra 20 in the afternoon for job applications. I’ll run out early.
Thanks for being honest. How are you sleeping, and are you drinking to help with sleep? Any racing heart, chest pain or fainting?
Four hours. Three or four beers at night. Heart races sometimes. No pain or fainting.
And how’s your mood since the redundancy — any thoughts of harming yourself?
I feel useless sometimes. But no, I’ve got my girlfriend and my brother.

Let me be clear about the prescription. Shared care is an agreement between a specialist service and a GP. In our area, the NHS only supports it with NHS-commissioned ADHD services, so I can’t take over from your private clinic. That isn’t me doubting your diagnosis.
model.why: Clear, reasoned decline without doubting the patient

model.text: So I’m being punished for not waiting four years?

I understand why it feels like that. What I can do today is refer you through Right to Choose to an NHS-funded adult ADHD provider. They may accept your diagnosis after their own review, and then we can share your care on the NHS.
model.why: Offers the NHS route the same day

model.text: Until then, your private clinic stays responsible for the prescription — please tell them about the redundancy; some can help with costs. The extra doses worry me: they push your pulse up, which was already 88, affect sleep and build tolerance. Can I let your psychiatrist know?
model.why: Bridging responsibility; extra dosing; consent to inform prescriber

model.text: Yes, OK. I didn’t think it mattered.
Beer helps you fall asleep but wakes you up later — let’s try cutting that down and taking the capsule early. I’ll also send details of advice on benefits after redundancy.

So: referral today, you speak to your clinic, no extra doses, and I’ll call you in two weeks about sleep and mood. If you ever feel unsafe, call 111 or the Samaritans on 116 123. What will you do first?
Ring the clinic about money, stick to one a day, and wait for the referral. Thanks — I thought you’d just say no.

social.t: Private treatment costs become unaffordable after job loss; that pressure can drive unsafe self-management.
Long NHS waits push people to private care; acknowledging this reduces conflict.

legal.t: Lisdexamfetamine is a Schedule 2 controlled drug (Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001); supply and record rules apply.

professional.t: GPs may decline shared care they are not competent or commissioned to provide; they must explain their reasons and ensure the patient knows how to obtain care.
Apply the local policy consistently; document the request, the decision and the alternatives offered.

community.t: Citizens Advice for benefits after redundancy; ADHD UK and AADD-UK; local Talking Therapies if mood worsens.

redFlags: Taking more than prescribed; running out early
Chest pain, palpitations, syncope, raised pulse or BP
Low mood or suicidal thoughts after job loss
ice: Concern: can’t afford it; losing the benefit

playbook.diagnosis: A shared care request from a non-commissioned private provider, with emerging safety concerns (extra dosing, sleep, alcohol, tachycardia, weight loss) after redundancy.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “I can’t take over this particular arrangement, but I can get you onto the NHS route today — and I’m worried about the extra doses and the sleep.”

management.reflectIce: “You expected me to take over because you can’t afford it any more. I can’t do that directly, but the referral is the way to NHS prescriptions.”
management.psychosocial: Financial advice after redundancy; partner support; mood check.
sharedPlan: Private provider remains prescriber until transfer — he contacts them about costs
No extra doses; inform private psychiatrist with consent
safetyNet: Chest pain, fainting or palpitations that do not settle → urgent care
Call earlier if supply runs out

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by an unexplained “no”, or by a “yes” to keep him happy.

items.fail: Agrees to prescribe “just this month” without shared care in place.
items.why: Prescribing a controlled drug without specialist support, monitoring arrangements or a commissioned pathway breaks local policy and GMC prescribing principles.
items.fix: Explain the decision and arrange the NHS route; keep the private prescriber responsible until transfer.

items.fail: Implies online private diagnoses are unreliable.
items.why: He becomes defensive and the safety issues stay hidden.
items.fix: Separate the policy from the person: “This isn’t about doubting your diagnosis.”

items.fail: Never asks how he takes the medicine.
items.why: Extra dosing, sleep loss and alcohol use are missed.
items.fix: Ask neutrally about dosing, sleep, alcohol and side effects.

timeMap.d: Identity and privacy; hear the request.
Why now (redundancy); how he takes it; sleep, alcohol, heart symptoms; mood.
Explain the decline and the reasons; offer Right to Choose today.
Private provider remains responsible; extra doses; inform prescriber; alcohol and sleep; financial help.

wordPics.clearFail: Refuses abruptly and ends the call, or agrees to prescribe outside any shared care framework; no exploration of dosing or mood.
wordPics.fail: Declines correctly but offers no NHS route or explanation, or misses the extra dosing and alcohol.
wordPics.pass: Declines with clear reasons, refers via Right to Choose, clarifies who prescribes in the meantime, and addresses the extra doses and sleep.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus finds the redundancy early, keeps him on side without doubting the diagnosis, screens mood, informs the prescriber with consent, and arranges a follow-up call.

avoid.instead: “You’re our NHS patient — I can’t take over this private arrangement, but here is the NHS route.”
avoid.why: He is entitled to NHS care; only the private arrangement is declined.

avoid.instead: “The NHS service will do its own review — that’s standard.”

avoid.dont: “Just this once I’ll do a script.”
avoid.instead: “Your clinic stays responsible until the NHS team takes over.”
avoid.why: Ad hoc controlled-drug prescribing outside shared care is unsafe.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Follows “from this month”, “I can’t keep paying” and “I’ll run out early”.
Idea (shared care is automatic); concern (losing the medicine that changed his life, money); expectation (an NHS prescription from this month).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — he has lost his job and cannot afford private prescriptions; he is taking extra doses, sleeping four hours and drinking to sleep; he fears losing the medicine that “changed his life” — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
